source_text: Κοινὸς γὰρ αὐτῶν πατὴρ ὁ Θεὸς, καὶ ἀδελφοὶ πάντες, οὐκ ἀπὸ ἑνὸς καὶ μιᾶς γεννηθέντες, ἀλλ' ἐκ τῆς υἱοθεσίας τοῦ Πνεύματος εἰς τὴν διὰ τῆς ἀγάπης ὁμόνοιαν ἀλλήλοις συναρμοσθέντες. Χορὸς ἕτοιμος, προσθήκη μεγάλη τῶν ἀπ' αἰῶνος δοξαζόντων τὸν Κύριον, οὐ καθ' ἕνα συναθροισθέντες, ἀλλ' ἀθρόως μετατεθέντες. Τίς δὲ ὁ τρόπος τῆς μεταθέσεως; Οὗτοι, μεγέθει σώματος, καὶ ἡλικίας ἀκμῇ, καὶ δυνάμει τῶν καθ' ἑαυτοὺς ἁπάντων διενεγκόντες, εἰς τοὺς στρατιωτικοὺς τελεῖν ἐτάχθησαν καταλόγους· καὶ δι' ἐμ πειρίαν πολεμικὴν, καὶ ἀνδρείαν ψυχῆς, ἤδη τὰς πρώτας εἶχον παρὰ βασιλέων τιμὰς, ὀνομα στοὶ παρὰ πᾶσιν ὄντες δι' ἀρετήν. Ἐπειδὴ δὲ περιηγγέλη τὸ ἄθεον ἐκεῖνο καὶ ἀσε βὲς κήρυγμα, μὴ ὁμολογεῖν τὸν Χριστὸν, ἢ κινδύνους ἐκδέχεσθαι· ἠπειλεῖτο δὲ πᾶν εἶδος κολάσεως, καὶ πολὺς ὁ θυμὸς καὶ θηριώδης παρὰ τῶν κριτῶν τῆς ἀδικίας κατὰ τῶν εὐσεβούντων κεκίνητο· ἐπιβουλαὶ δὲ καὶ δόλοι κατ' αὐτῶν συνεῤῥάπτοντο, καὶ ποικίλα εἴδη βασάνων ἐπετηδεύετο, καὶ οἱ αἰκιζόμενοι ἀπαραίτητοι, τὸ πῦρ ἕτοιμον, τὸ ξίφος ἠκόνητο, ὁ σταυρὸς ἐπεπήγει· ὁ βόθρος, ὁ τροχὸς, αἱ μάστιγες· οἱ μὲν ἔφευγον, οἱ δὲ ὑπέκυπτον, οἱ δὲ ἐσαλεύοντο· τινὲς δὲ πρὸ τῆς πείρας μόνην τὴν ἀπειλὴν κατεπλάγησαν· ἕτεροι δὲ, ἐγγὺς γενόμενοι τῶν δεινῶν, ἰλιγγίασαν· ἄλλοι δὲ, τοῖς ἀγῶσιν ἐμβάντες, εἶτα διαρκέσαι πρὸς τὸ πέρας τῶν πόνων ἀδυνατήσαντες, περὶ τὰ μέσα που τῆς ἀθλήσεως ἀπειπόντες, ὥσπερ οἱ ἐν πελάγει χειμαζόμενοι, καὶ ἃ εἶχον ἤδη ἀγώγιμα τῆς ὑπομονῆς ἐναυάγησαν· τότε δὴ οὗτοι, οἱ ἀήττη τοι καὶ γενναῖοι τοῦ Χριστοῦ στρατιῶται, παρελθόν τες εἰς μέσους, ἐπιδεικνύντος τοῦ ἄρχοντος τὰ βασι λέως γράμματα καὶ τὴν ὑπακοὴν ἀπαιτοῦντος, ἐλευ θέρᾳ τῇ φωνῇ, εὐθαρσῶς καὶ ἀνδρείως, οὐδὲν ὑπο πτήξαντες τῶν ὁρωμένων, οὐδὲ καταπλαγέντες τὰ ἀπειλούμενα, Χριστιανοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ἀνεκήρυξαν. Ὦ μακάριαι γλῶσσαι, ὅσαι τὴν ἱερὰν ἐκείνην ἀφῆκαν φωνὴν, ἣν ἀὴρ μὲν δεξάμενος ἡγιάσθη, ἄγγελοι δὲ ἀκούσαντες ἐπεκρότησαν· διάβολος δὲ μετὰ δαι μόνων ἐτραυματίσθη· Κύριος δὲ ἐν οὐρανοῖς ἀπεγράψατο. Εἶπον τοίνυν ἕκαστος εἰς τὸ μέσον παριών· Χριστιανός εἰμι. Καὶ ὥσπερ ἐν τοῖς σταδίοις οἱ ἐπ' ἄθλησιν παροδεύοντες ὁμοῦ τε λέγουσιν ἑαυτῶν τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸν τόπον τῆς ἀγωνίας μεθ ίστανται· οὕτω δὴ καὶ οὗτοι τότε, ῥίψαντες τὰς ἀπὸ γενέσεως αὐτοῖς ἐπιφημισθείσας προσηγορίας, ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ Σωτῆρος ἕκαστος ἑαυτὸν ἀνηγόρευον. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐποίουν ἅπαντες, τῷ προλαβόντι ἑαυτὸν συνάπτων ὁ ἐφεξῆς. Ὥστε ἐγένετο πάντων προσηγορία μία· οὐκέτι γὰρ ὁ δεῖνα, ἢ ὁ δεῖνα, ἀλλὰ Χριστιανοὶ πάντες ἀνεκηρύττοντο. Τί οὖν ὁ κρατῶν τότε; Δεινὸς γὰρ ἦν καὶ ποικίλος, τὰ μὲν θωπείαις ὑπελθεῖν, τὰ δὲ ἀπειλαῖς παρατρέψαι. Πρῶτον μὲν αὐτοὺς κατεγοήτευε ταῖς θωπείαις, τὸν τόνον τῆς εὐσεβείας παραλύειν πειρώμενος. Μὴ προδῶτε ὑμῶν τὴν νεότητα· μηδὲ θάνατον ἄωρον τῆς ἡδείας ταύτης ζωῆς διαμείψητε. Ἄτοπον γὰρ τοὺς ἐν τοῖς πολέμοις ἀριστεύειν συνειθισμένους τὸν τῶν κακούργων θάνα τον ἀποθνήσκειν. Πρὸς τούτοις χρήματα ὑπισχνεῖτο. Τὰ δὲ ἐδίδου, τιμὰς ἐκ βασιλέως, καὶ ἀξιωμάτων διανομὰς, καὶ μυρίαις αὐτοὺς ἐπινοίαις κατεστρατήγει, Ὡς δὲ οὐκ ἐνεδίδοσαν πρὸς τὴν πεῖραν ταύ την, ἐπὶ τὸ ἕτερον εἶδος τῆς μηχανῆς μετῄει.
thought_title: The Forty's bold confession before the ruler
orientation: Basil has just described the martyrs' common spiritual lineage and now turns to narrate how these forty soldiers, summoned before the ruler, publicly declared themselves Christians despite threats and temptations.
pass_a_gloss: For their common father is God, and all are brothers, not begotten from one man and one woman, but from the adoption of the Spirit, fitted together to one another into the unity of mind through love. A ready company, a great addition to those who from eternity glorify the Lord, not gathered one by one, but removed all at once. And what was the manner of the removal? These men, having excelled all those of their own age in size of body and prime of life and strength, were ordered to serve in the military rolls; and through experience in war and courage of soul, they already held the first honors from kings, being renowned among all for virtue. But when that godless and impious proclamation was circulated, not to confess Christ, or to await dangers; and every kind of punishment was threatened, and great and beastly wrath was stirred up by the judges of injustice against the devout; and plots and deceits were stitched together against them, and various kinds of tortures were devised, and the tormentors were inexorable, the fire ready, the sword sharpened, the cross fixed; the pit, the wheel, the scourges; some fled, some bowed down, some were shaken; and some before the trial were terrified by the threat alone; and others, having come near the terrors, grew dizzy; and others, having entered the contests, then being unable to endure to the end of the pains, having given up somewhere around the middle of the contest, like those storm-tossed on the open sea, shipwrecked even the cargo of endurance which they already had; then indeed these men, the unconquered and noble soldiers of Christ, having come forward into the midst, while the ruler displayed the king's letters and demanded obedience, with free voice, boldly and courageously, cowering at nothing of what was seen, nor terrified at what was threatened, proclaimed themselves Christians. O blessed tongues, as many as sent forth that sacred voice, which the air receiving was sanctified, and angels hearing applauded; and the devil with demons was wounded; and the Lord in heaven recorded it. Each one then said, coming forward into the midst: I am a Christian. And just as in the stadiums those passing by for the contest both say their own names and move to the place of the struggle; so indeed these men then, having cast away the names given to them from birth, each one announced himself from the common Savior. And all did this, each one joining himself to the one who preceded him. So that there came to be one name of all; for no longer so-and-so, or so-and-so, but all were proclaimed Christians. What then did the ruler do at that time? For he was terrible and crafty, on the one hand to come upon them with flatteries, on the other to turn them aside with threats. First he bewitched them with flatteries, trying to loosen the tension of their devotion. Do not betray your youth; nor exchange an untimely death for this sweet life. For it is absurd that those accustomed to excel in wars should die the death of criminals. In addition to these things he promised money. And he gave some things, honors from the king, and distributions of offices, and he out-generaled them with countless schemes. But when they did not yield to this attempt, he moved to the other kind of device.

choices.why: The compound means same-mindedness; 'unity of mind' preserves the mental component and avoids the weaker 'harmony'.
ἀθρόως means collectively, in a body; 'removed' keeps the transfer sense of μετατίθημι without implying a single physical motion.
The glossary mandates 'contest' for ἄθλησις; the genitive marks the midpoint of the martyrdom struggle.
The verb is nautical; rendering it as a verb preserves the metaphor of losing the cargo of endurance at sea.
τόνος means tension or tone; 'tension' keeps the physical metaphor of slackening a stretched cord, and εὐσέβεια is rendered 'devotion' per glossary.
The verb means to defeat by stratagem; the compound rendering preserves the military metaphor Basil uses for the ruler's schemes.

pass_b_english: For their common Father is God, and they are all brothers—not born from one man and one woman, but fitted together into unity of mind with one another through the adoption of the Spirit and through love. They are a company made ready, a great addition to those who from eternity have glorified the Lord, not gathered one by one, but removed all at once. And what was the manner of their removal? These men, who excelled all their contemporaries in bodily size, in the prime of life, and in strength, were enrolled in the military registers. Because of their experience in war and their courage of soul, they already held the first honors from the emperors, and were famous among all for their virtue. But when that godless and impious proclamation was announced—that they must not confess Christ, or else face dangers—every kind of punishment was threatened, and great and beastly fury was stirred up by the judges of injustice against the devout. Plots and deceits were stitched together against them, and varied forms of torture were devised. The torturers were relentless: fire was made ready, the sword was sharpened, the cross was planted, the pit, the wheel, the whips. Some fled, some bowed down, some were shaken. Some, before the test, were terrified by the threat alone. Others, when they came near the horrors, grew dizzy. Still others entered the contests, but then, unable to endure to the end of their labors, gave up somewhere around the middle of the contest. Like men storm-tossed on the open sea, they shipwrecked even the cargo of endurance they already carried. Then these men—the unconquered and noble soldiers of Christ—came forward into the midst. The ruler displayed the emperor's letters and demanded obedience, but with a free voice, boldly and courageously, shrinking from nothing they saw and terrified by nothing threatened, they proclaimed themselves Christians. O blessed tongues, how many uttered that sacred sound! The air received it and was sanctified; the angels heard it and applauded; the devil and his demons were wounded; and the Lord recorded it in heaven. So each one came forward into the midst and said, "I am a Christian." And just as in the stadiums those who pass by for a contest speak their names and then move to the place of struggle, so these men then cast away the names given them at birth and each one announced himself by the name of the common Savior. And they all did this, each one joining himself to the one who had gone before. So there came to be one name for all of them: no longer "so-and-so" or "so-and-so," but all were proclaimed Christians. What then did the ruler do? He was clever and versatile, seeking to win them over at one moment with flattery and at another to turn them aside with threats. First he bewitched them with flattery, trying to slacken the tension of their devotion. "Do not betray your youth," he said, "and do not exchange this sweet life for an untimely death. It is absurd for men accustomed to excelling in wars to die the death of criminals." In addition to this he promised money. He offered honors from the emperor, distributions of offices, and out-generaled them with countless schemes. But when they did not yield to this attempt, he moved on to the other kind of device.

last_rejected.fix: not gathered one by one, but transferred all at once
last_rejected.ruling: μετατεθέντες means 'transferred/removed'; 'removed' is within normal range, no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: that they must not confess Christ, or else face dangers
last_rejected.source_quote: μὴ ὁμολογεῖν τὸν Χριστὸν, ἢ κινδύνους ἐκδέχεσθαι
last_rejected.why: ἐκδέχεσθαι means 'await/expect', not 'face'; dangers are the consequence of confessing, not alternative
last_rejected.fix: not to confess Christ, but to await dangers
last_rejected.ruling: ἐκδέχεσθαι includes 'face/encounter'; 'or else face dangers' correctly conveys the alternative threat.

last_rejected.why: οὐδὲ = 'nor', continuing negation; 'terrified by nothing' misreads as double negative
last_rejected.fix: nor terrified by what was threatened
last_rejected.ruling: οὐδὲ καταπλαγέντες = 'nor being terrified'; 'terrified by nothing threatened' conveys same meaning adequately.

last_rejected.quote: how many uttered that sacred sound
last_rejected.source_quote: ὅσαι τὴν ἱερὰν ἐκείνην ἀφῆκαν φωνήν
last_rejected.why: ὅσαι = 'as many as' (exclamatory), not 'how many' questioning; ἀφῆκαν = 'let loose/uttered'
last_rejected.fix: O blessed tongues, all those that let loose that sacred voice
last_rejected.ruling: ὅσαι is exclamatory 'how many/blessed tongues that'; 'how many uttered' captures the exclamation adequately.

last_rejected.why: κατεστρατήγει is imperfect, describing ongoing action, not completed; 'out-generaled' suggests success
last_rejected.fix: he was outmaneuvering them with countless schemes
last_rejected.ruling: κατεστρατήγει imperfect can be rendered 'out-generaled'; tense nuance is minor, not a major error.
